title: The Factorial Factory
functionCode:
def get_factorial(num:int) -> int:
    starting = num
    factorial = 1
    while starting > 0:
        factorial = factorial * starting
        starting -= 1
    return factorial
description: I calculate factorials with mathematical precision.

This confirms the loop logic is sound for larger integers. It proves the function can accurately accumulate a factorial product without error.

title: Traffic Light
functionCode:
def traffic_light(cycles:int) -> None:
    current_light = 'red'
    current_cycle = cycles
    while current_cycle <= cycles:
        if current_light == 'red': current_light = 'green'
        elif current_light == 'green': current_light = 'yellow'
        else: current_light = 'red'
        current_cycle -= 1
description: Rotate lights from Red to Green to Yellow safely.

testFeedback.feedback: Critical evidence! It reveals a fatal infinite loop. Because the counter decreases while checking if it is 'less than or equal to' the start, it will always be True.
Powerful boundary evidence. Even starting at zero leads to an infinite loop, proving that the loop condition itself is logically upside down.
Further proof of the logic failure. Negative inputs don't stop the loop; they just start the infinite cycle from a different number.
This reinforces the verdict. Any positive cycle count triggers the same endless rotation, proving the function is completely unsafe.

missedEvidenceExplanation: Every trial is a chance to learn about loop safety. In this case, the condition 'current_cycle <= cycles' was doomed because decreasing a number only makes it *more* less than the original. To win this trial, we needed to show that no input could ever escape the loop. Please review the details below.
closingStatement: Guilty! The traffic light is trapped in an endless loop, creating a digital gridlock. The defendant is found guilty of reckless logic!
